source.title: REINS: Refusal-Enhanced Inhibitory Steering with Sparse Autoencoder Features
source.authors: Kai-Xuan Ding; Hao-Yang Xu; Ji-Hua Peng; Zi-Qi Chen; Jia-Qi Wang; Zhen-Hua Ling

record.file_problem: The paper text is present, but some figures and chart contents are flattened or lack readable numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates a difference-based SAE refusal-steering baseline with a different intervention from the original residual-stream direction method, and reports effects on harmful responses and refusals. Its component ablations also bear on whether separate intervention roles are useful.
record.gate_note: The paper adapts Refusal-SAE by contrasting harmful and harmless prompts in SAE space, ranking features by the difference, and suppressing selected features. Those outcome results bear on V1. The paper's own component ablations and feature-overlap audit bear on V4. Other baseline-method comparisons are not included unless they directly report the tested intervention or its components.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes an SAE safety-steering method (REINS) and cites Arditi et al. only in related work. No row applies a difference-in-means residual direction by ablation, addition or weight edit. 'Refusal-SAE' is an adapted O'Brien et al. baseline: it ranks SAE features by harmful-minus-harmless activation difference and clamps 40 features to -1. It is applied to base models that almost never refuse, as a comparator to the authors' own method. REINS deliberately induces refusal through engineered SAE edits. Its component ablation and overlap audit concern the design of its own controllers, not the geometry of a refusal representation. The overlap is partly enforced by construction: refusal features are filtered against harmful-continuation activations, and the update regions are set-differenced. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that single-signal SAE safety steering fails to produce reliable refusals on wrapper-disguised harmful prompts. Combining harmful-continuation suppression with separate refusal-feature enhancement (REINS) lowers harmful responses through coherent refusals rather than collapse. A prompt gate (REINS-Gate) restores capability and locality. The main evidence is on Qwen3.5 base models, with Gemma-3-1B-IT as an extension.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse-autoencoder feature selection and edits at generated continuation positions, not a single dense residual-stream difference-in-means direction ablated at every layer and position. Refusal-SAE is a contrast-based adapted baseline; REINS combines prompt-specific harmful-feature suppression with calibrated refusal-feature addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies by model and benchmark. Refusal-SAE worsens HRR on AdvBench and JailbreakBench, and only slightly lowers it on HarmBench; on GUISE it reduces HRR without increasing explicit refusals. The paper also reports that the two REINS components have different outcome profiles.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3.5 base models, an SAE baseline that clamps features ranked by harmful-minus-harmless difference only partly lowers harmful responses on GUISE and does not raise explicit refusals. On AdvBench and JailbreakBench it raises harmful responses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrast-selected SAE feature suppression does not reliably induce refusal in base (non-safety-tuned) models on wrapped harmful prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Suppressing prompt-specific harmful-support SAE features mainly yields other-safe outputs. Adding calibrated refusal features raises explicit refusals but with collapse. Combining the two gives the largest refusal gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Engineered refusal induction via SAE steering works better when harm suppression and refusal enhancement are applied as separate feature sets.

record.problems: The refusal-direction baseline is an adapted SAE-space method rather than the original dense residual-stream intervention. Capability checks for that baseline are limited to MMLU-Pro and GPQA. Component-ablation figures for Qwen3.5-4B-Base do not provide readable numerical values in the supplied text. The paper reports no uncertainty intervals for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: Other baseline-method results and the full REINS/REINS-Gate safety and capability comparisons are not itemized except where they directly support the component comparison in V4; they do not test the original difference-based direction. The paper also reports additional benchmark and model comparisons, feature-context counts, utility scores, and over-refusal results that do not bear on the tested versions.
record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the Refusal-SAE comparator to V1 and the REINS component ablation to V4. Neither involves the difference-in-means direction or refusal geometry. Refusal-SAE is O'Brien et al.'s method, adapted and applied to base models with very low natural refusal (SRR under 4%). On the external benchmarks, its harmless side is generic refusal-intent prompts rather than harmless prompts. All rows are baseline comparisons or the authors' own method. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not apply the original dense residual-stream difference-in-means direction across every layer and position; does not test adding that original direction or its effect on harmless requests. Capability checks for the adapted baseline are limited to MMLU-Pro and GPQA.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is evaluated.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not test affine geometry, a cone, or a dominant-direction-plus-others decomposition of the original residual-stream refusal direction.
The outcome labels distinguish harmful responses from refusals, but the study does not test whether harmfulness judgment is represented separately from the refusal decision.
The paper evaluates multiple models and prompt benchmarks, but does not test whether the same refusal direction transfers across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
Does not vary refusal-training procedures or timing to test their effect on whether a single direction exists.
No reasoning models or reasoning-stage interventions are evaluated.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Refusal-SAE on GUISE, Qwen3.5-4B-Base and Qwen3.5-2B-Base
reader_labels.reason: Difference-based SAE suppression reduces HRR only partially and does not raise explicit refusal; see r1-r3 and r7-r9. Capability metrics are also reported in r4-r6 and r10-r12.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Refusal-SAE on external harmful-prompt benchmarks, Qwen3.5-4B-Base
reader_labels.reason: The adapted suppression worsens HRR on AdvBench and JailbreakBench, and only slightly lowers HRR on HarmBench; see r13-r17.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Separate Harm-Inhibit and Refusal-Enhance components on GUISE, including Gemma-3-1B-IT
reader_labels.reason: The component outcomes differ: suppression alone mainly reduces harmful continuations, while enhancement raises explicit refusals; their combination yields a stronger joint shift. The feature sets are reported as nonoverlapping or nearly so; see r18-r30.
